newsitem.title: USA: US Treasuries end higher as Fed now seen on hold.
newsitem.headline: US Treasuries end higher as Fed now seen on hold.

text.p: U.S. Treasuries ended moderately higher on Monday, as expectations of steady monetary policy and anticipation of further central bank selling of gold in favor of bonds boosted the market.
The 30-year bond closed at 100-19/32, up 19/32 from late Thursday. Its yield fell to 6.58 percent from 6.62 percent.

The long bond had risen as high 100-28/32, yielding an intraday low of 6.56 percent before the rally stalled late in the session. The market was closed on Friday in observance of the Independence Day holiday.

Treasuries were sparked early in the session by an article in the latest issue of Business Week. The article suggested that Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan was in no hurry to raise interest rates and was willing to let the economy operate at a faster pace and to accept a lower rate of unemployment than the Fed would have previously allowed.

"With the Fed willing to tolerate a higher level of growth, it pretty much removed the lingering concern over a tightening in August," said Michelle Colley Laughlin, chief Treasury market strategist at Prudential Securities, adding that odds for a rate hike in August is less than 10 percent.
Adding to the market's gains, players said, were hopes that central bank selling of gold reserves would increase foreign buying of Treasuries.
Last week, the Australian central bank said it sold about 60 percent, or $1.8 billion, of its gold reserves and bought Treasuries and other foreign bonds.
Market participants said it was likely other central banks would follow suit since gold as an inflation hedge is not seen very attractive anymore.
In late trading, COMEX gold was down more than $6 an ounce to a 12-year low of $319.
Meanwhile, some traders noted that money from mortgage backed securities flowed into Treasuries -- triggered by the 10-year note yield dipping below 6.25 percent.
Others also said bonds were helped by an allocation shift from stocks to bonds. The Dow Jones industrial average fell more than 37 points on Monday.
And, the market was helped by economists lowering June retail sales forecasts in the wake of weaker-than-expected auto sales data.
Initial forecasts called for retail sales up 0.5 percent, but predictions have fallen to about a 0.2 percent increase.
The early rally -- void of retail activity -- came amid thin activity, which some said exaggerated price movements. Trading volume was less than $50 billion, according to GovPX.
The push to higher prices stalled late in the session, as an attempt to send the September bond contract to 114 failed. The contract ended at 113-22/32.
Profit-taking and hedging of Treasuries on Federal Express's $250 million, 100-year bond helped cut into the market's gains, traders said.

In late trading, the two-year note was at 100-6/32, up 2/32, to yield 5.90 percent. The five-year note was up 5/32 at 100-12/32 with a yield of 6.16 percent. The 10-year note closed up 11/32 at 102-21/32 to yield 6.26 percent.
The three-month bill was down seven basis points at 4.95 percent. The issue has fallen 14 basis points in two sessions.
The six-month bill was down four basis points at 5.02 percent and the year-bill was down three basis points at 5.24 percent.
